title: Sword and pen
hook: a warrior who was also a poet, in the same hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, holding debates kindly: views on the Dasam Granth held side by side, and the shared code keeping practice steady. Your line was disagree kindly. Did you say their view back fairly? Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

A hand that has held a bowstring all afternoon picks up a pen at night. The fingers are sore. There's a battle behind and probably another ahead. And the pen moves anyway: praise of the Timeless One, a story of his own life, a ballad, a letter to an emperor. Today, step back from the writings of Guru Gobind Singh and look at the hand itself. The same hand held both.
screen: `A BOWSTRING BY DAY.` → `A PEN BY NIGHT.` → `THE SAME HAND HELD BOTH.`

segments.voice: Sikhs have a name for this pairing: sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier. A sant is a person of devotion. A sipahi is a soldier. The ideal is one person who is both at once, not a soldier on weekdays and a saint on holy days. Think back over the block. The Bachitar Natak tells of battle in verse. The Zafarnama is a letter of rebuke, but it opens with praise of God. And there's a verse, from a composition in the Dasam Granth, that gathers the two halves into a single plea. Paraphrased, as Sikhs read it, it asks God for a gift: that I never turn away from doing good; that when I go out to face the enemy I have no fear and win; that I teach my own mind to long for Your praise; and that when my time comes, I die fighting in the thick of battle. Listen to the order of it. Doing good comes first. Courage follows. The mind's longing for praise sits right in the middle. And only then the sword. The fighting is for something, and the something is written first. Look at Sikh life now and the pairing is still there. A Khalsa Sikh keeps the kirpan, a small sword, as an article of faith, and may carry a prayer book, a gutka, close by too. Neither one cancels the other. In this reading, the pen without the sword could be words with no backbone. The sword without the pen, a strength with no reason. He kept them in one hand.
screen: `SANT-SIPAHI: THE SAINT-SOLDIER.` · `PRAISE AND BATTLE IN ONE BLOCK.` · `NEVER TURN AWAY FROM DOING GOOD.` · `THE KIRPAN AND THE GUTKA.` · then, large: `PEN AND SWORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a short poem. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you'd stand up for, even when it costs you: a person, a principle, a place. Now find two or four plain lines about it. No rhyme needed. Not a prayer, just your own words about what you'd defend. Write them down if you can; if not, say them over in your head. Then sit with them quietly until the bell, and notice which line feels strongest. The bell holds the time.
Sword and pen. Guru Gobind Singh as sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier: devotion and courage held by one person, with doing good written first. Today's word.
Your line: pen and sword. Today, carry your little poem with you, and if the moment comes to stand up for that thing, let the words go first. Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Khalsa Sikhs keep the kirpan as an article of faith alongside daily prayer, and the ideal of the sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier, is taught in gurdwaras and Sikh homes.

fork.reveal: doing good comes first, then courage and the longing for praise, and only last the battle.
